title: Notes of Ministry - 87 - February 1980

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 87 - February 1 (2495)/Notes of Ministry - 87 - Februa - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I want to speak briefly about oneness. A mighty company of people had one heart to make David king; two sisters, in a place where conditions were happy, were enjoined to be of the same mind; and a company of princes, representing all the tribes of Israel, had a single thought in bringing for God the dedication-gift of the altar and offerings in abundance. It is a lovely assembly feature at which the bitterness of Satan’s attack is constantly aiming—

oneness, unity of thought, unity of purpose, singleness of heart and mind as to what is precious to Christ. It is a favourite tactic of the foe to begin and to continue to attack it. The attack may have small beginnings, but tends as the foe has place to lead to very grievous consequences.

It would seem from the Scriptures that this feature of oneness is a feature of sonship. The Lord would, it seems, have this in mind in what He said in John 17, “The glory which thou hast given me I have given them, that they may be one, as we are one” (John 17: 22). Sons characteristically will think as one in relation to what concerns their father. One of the dignities, I suppose, of a company in sonship is that they think the same thing and move in the same way, yet each brings in something by way of fragrant personality, which makes each one distinctive before God, though all move as one.

The writer of the Ephesian letter enjoins the saints to walk worthy of the calling wherewith we have been called; he then proceeds to speak of the unity of the Spirit, to be kept in the uniting bond of peace, as if the real character and experience of the calling would set us in oneness together as we are true to it (see Ephesians 4: 1–3). What a wonderful thing to be true to our place in sonship! .What a wonderful thing to be in the true experience and expression of the place and portion into which we have been called of God, bringing out in the company of the saints oneness of heart and mind as to everything.

This was no mean company of saints, typically, that came to anoint David king. If you read the earlier parts of the chapter, you see what a mighty throng this was, with one heart to make David king. How attractive David had become! Conflict had waged long, between David on the one hand and Saul on the other, and at every point of that conflict the attractiveness and moral worth of David had shone, leading to hearts being attached to him. The features of Saul, so degraded as we read of them, remind us, beloved brethren, of what our flesh is; the features of David attract us unerringly to Jesus, to Christ. This mighty throng was of one heart to make David king. Is there anyone here who would not yield Christ His place, His royal place and glory, His royal rights unchallenged? I verily believe every heart would be at one in this company to exalt Christ; that is the root of the whole matter of which we are speaking. If Christ has His place there must be oneness. If there is lack of oneness in any sense we are right in asking the question, and asking it as to ourselves, Has Christ His place?
Along with that is a cognate, necessary matter; Has the Holy Spirit, the one Spirit, His place?
Is there anything hindering the Spirit of God in His speaking and authority at any point, anywhere? It is the unity of the Spirit that is to be kept.

This is a remarkable scene where there are all these persons, men of war, persons of some eminence in Israel. The chapter makes most interesting reading in showing what had risen up in support of David, despite the influence of Saul working away in Israel. This is what is to be happening, and it is what I believe, thank God, is happening. Let us attend to this matter of the place Christ has; may this favourite tactic that Satan has so often sought to employ, sometimes, alas, with a certain success, not again get headway. Oneness of heart and, following that, oneness of mind and thought in relation to divine things, are to be substantially found among those who love Him.

Let us think of this starting point, in which every heart in Israel is committed. It says, “all of them men of war” first, then “all the rest of Israel were of one heart to make David king”. Let us see that the glory of an exalted Christ is an operative point amongst us, so that we are affected by it. It is not merely assenting to the features of His glory as we dwell upon them, but being affected by the exaltation of Christ. His place up there at God’s right hand becoming powerfully operative to affect the whole outlook in which we move together; “one heart to make David king”.

It was evidently a matter of sorrow to the beloved apostle that there were two sisters in Philippi, two named persons, whom he felt necessary to enjoin to be of the same mind in the Lord. It would no doubt strike right home to these two dear sisters as this letter came to Philippi. What a sister there had been in Philippi in Lydia! What a place the beloved sisters have in the working out

of what is precious to Christ. It is not an audible place in the gatherings of the saints, but a place, I would say soberly, of very great influence for Christ and in His interests. That is what the beloved sisters have. You think of Lydia and the way she received Paul in Philippi, the Lord having opened her heart to attend to the things spoken by Paul. Manifestly she did attend to the things spoken by Paul and brought out some fitting expression in answer to them in herself. So that Paul and Silas afterwards “came to Lydia” a lovely expression that is—as if there was something with that beloved sister that furnished a basis for God to bring in increase in that city, as He evidently did.

Now Paul has to speak to two; he does not speak negatively, nor does he speak in any sense accusingly. He just exhorts these two sisters “to be of the same mind in the Lord”. The skill of that is manifest; the uniting touch of it is manifest. How thankful we would be to show this touch of skill which the beloved apostle shows. He did not attempt to discriminate between them, which he would not be ready to do in the position in which he was, but he enjoined them to be of the same mind in the Lord. What a conversation this would, I judge, produce between these two sisters, which would search out the whole position. If there was a bad spirit with one of them, it would show itself. If I were the one of them at fault, it would show itself. Some misunderstanding that had led to some kind of discord between them would show itself. The power of this exhortation from the beloved apostle, from such a man as he was, would open out the whole situation between those two sisters, and they would get right, whatever that involved.

It is the skill given of God to this beloved writer that touches this matter positively before it develops, before a major difference of judgment comes in. The difference, based maybe on some small matter initially, might tend to set the saints on the one hand or the other hand in respect of it; the skill that comes in to meet the matter, whilst it is yet of small consequence in the general position, is a masterly point which we should see. Let me ask myself, let me ask everyone here, Have we any element of difference with anyone? Is there something which the enemy could use to damage what is so precious to Christ, to hinder the substantial expression of the assembly for the delight of His heart? Is there any such thing? Let us get right. The Spirit of Christ will operate so that matters may be got right. The whole point in the assembly is to get everything right.

And there is the means in the headship of Christ and the supply of the Spirit to get everything right. The assembly is furnished in view of maintaining, and constantly maintaining, what is right in the sight of God. This gives so wonderful a basis for God to go on and expand in the hearts of the saints His greatest matters.
There are differences between these cases, but the point here is that it is just two sisters. The thing has not, it seems, reached great proportions yet, but it might reach great proportions.
The apostle meets it. Let us be watchful, dear brethren, as to any intrusion that would lead to the least estrangement, far less bitterness, between any one of us and any one of the rest of us.

Let us be watchful (a matter in which the Lord and the one Spirit would help us) that nothing may come into the economy of local assemblies that would hinder the progress of what is dear to Christ, responsive to His heart, and representative of Himself in the course of the testimony.

In Numbers 7 there was a rich answer to God in the dedication of the altar and the dedication-gift of the altar, related as they are to the service of God and the setting up and sustaining of that service. We have the gifts that were brought by the twelve princes, and as you read down the long chapter (even though it seems to be at the cost of repetition) every prince’s offering is described. You find that they are substantial, but they are just the same; there is none greater than any other. The offerings of the princes in relation to the dedication of the altar stand together, as if they are all supporting the setting up of the service of God.

A prince is a very attractive thought, involving for the saints nobility of a heavenly kind. You read of saints in one place being more noble than the saints in another place for a stated reason (Acts 17: 11). I come back to the point again of the dignity of sonship, which enters into this because the prince is a son. Think of our calling, marked out beforehand for adoption through Jesus Christ to the Father. Think, too, of the immensity of divine thoughts, reaching right back before time, and the bringing into expression of them through the grace of the Spirit in this time of reviving in which we are. Where things are on the line just of what is religious—I speak in the widest sense—very little is known, if anything, of sonship. It is where Christ has His place, and where a spirit of adoption, the Spirit of God’s Son, has place, that the saints are brought into the experience of sonship. The experience of sonship is the basis for bringing out the features of sonship into expression. We long that they may not only appear but increasingly appear and have their due place in the circle of those who love Christ.

So there are the princes, distinguished persons, and they bring their offerings, and the offering of each prince is the same. There is great wealth—silver and gold, fine flour mingled with oil, incense in great volume; but the offerings are the same. The point of the scene is not exactly variety, it is to bring out this feature of oneness in the saints in reference to their links with God and what is due to Him in His service. What we read of is the immense aggregate of all these gifts. It is exactly the aggregate of the twelve princes’ gifts that you see in this section, as if the Spirit of God gathers it all up into one great volume of offering, accrediting it to all Israel, for His glory.

That is an immense suggestion, not in any way to militate against variety in the service itself; the suggestion is that the calling, the measure of the calling, gives the measure of the offering that is to accompany it. God receives a fitting answer in the oneness of movement in His beloved saints, in that which is particularly to bring out for His heart the preciousness of Christ, and the glory of the one offering by which our God has His cherished portion in those who love Him.

Well, dear brethren, may there be oneness, may there be unity of purpose, unity of heart, unity of thought—not seen in the affairs of men in our day. It is unobtainable in the affairs of men in general, for they have not Christ and they have not the Spirit; but we have Christ and we have the Spirit, and God would bring out this very precious feature of oneness among His saints. May there be an answer thus for Him, for His name’s sake.

The only connection that I see between these two scriptures relates to the reference to “the highways”—“they, in whose heart are the highways”. This is a beautiful psalm; it would relate to the time of Israel’s recovery. Scripture is full of the thought of Israel’s recovery.

What a day it is going to be for divine Persons!—a day that we ought to have in our thoughts and conversations. Those that love the Lord are interested in what He has in Israel and especially in the time of her recovery. The sons of Korah head the psalm, the idea of recovery and the basis of mercy. Everything is to be secured on that basis, whether now or then.
I am impressed with the attractive features that come into the psalm—“How amiable are thy tabernacles”, it says, and then it speaks about “the courts of Jehovah” and of appearing

“before God in Zion” and of “the house of my God”. These, dear brethren, are attractive features connected with the recovery. It is a privilege to know something of them, of a line of things that is unique to the time that we are in. These things which have been, and will be, literal in Israel highlight to us the greatest possible privileges of christianity—God’s tabernacles, and that He should desire to be near to man in undisturbed conditions. He is going to tabernacle with men in the day of God, yet to come, but He would have us to have these things in our hearts. The psalm speaks of what is in the heart, “the courts of

Jehovah”—what an attractive thought that is! Think of the saints gathering and assembling, as they did in those days past, assembling in “the courts of Jehovah”; “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather stand at the threshold of the house of my God, than dwell in the tents of wickedness”.

The way into these things is evidently through these verses 5 to 7. It speaks about “the valley of Baca” (‘weeping’) and it says, “Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee ... They go from strength to strength”. What a comfort it is to us, beloved brethren, that out of the greatest weakness and the greatest sorrow there should be the element of strength, strength that would lay hold on God. Circumstances naturally might seem impossible but “Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee—they, in whose heart are the highways ... They go from strength to strength—each one will appear before God in Zion”.

Divine highways are in these persons’ hearts. That would be the basis of the recovery in Israel’s day. The principles that applied then are the principles that apply now, that recovery is on the basis of divine principles; persons realising what is right and doing what is right is the basis of all recovery. These highways are in their heart. It is a remarkable thing that God had put them in their heart. It is not that they are coming back to conform to an order of rule exactly—although that is so, of course—but God works in the heart. He writes His law there; He writes it in hearts. It speaks to us, of course, of the necessity with us of having hearts that are material for the divine writing. This is what God would do by the Spirit; the apostle says that that is the way He works, and they (Israel) come back because divine principles are in their hearts.
That is the basis of Israel’s recovery and ours.

Now I wanted to refer to these four divine highways in 2 Timothy; these are the highways of the recovery—“righteousness, faith, love, peace”. There may be more, of course—there are more; but Paul gives us these in the very place where he speaks of the way of recovery.

Righteousness, I understand, is simply what is right. I think I got that from Mr. Newlands of this city many years ago and I do not think it can be bettered. It has been one of the great divine highways right from the start. The setting of things in order creationally demonstrated the great principle of righteousness in God’s mind—the sun and the moon and the stars, and the days and the times, are an illustration of the great feature of righteousness. Then as breakdown comes in in the history we have “righteous Abel” (Matthew 23: 35); we have a man at the very start marked off as being righteous. He did the only righteous thing that a man could do. Shut out of the garden, sin lying upon man, he comes to God with a sacrifice which spoke of Christ. He did what was right. Think of God looking upon him; it says that
“Jehovah looked upon Abel” (Genesis 4: 4); God saw there one man who understood His mind and did what was right.
We come to Abraham; the world in idolatry, away from God. God shut out, and false gods.

Abraham obeyed God. God called him and he obeyed. He did what was right. Of course, the Lord Jesus is the supreme scriptural example of it; He loved righteousness, suffered for righteousness, suffered because He would not be diverted—from what was right, “for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness”, Matthew 3: 15. As we all know, and it has often been said, the only right thing to do in the midst of the confusion of 2 Timothy days is to
“withdraw from iniquity” (2 Timothy 2: l9). That is
right; and to separate from vessels to dishonour, that is also right, the apostle sets it out for us.

We had a word here recently as to the way that the Lord had made provision for all time, for all the exigencies of the testimony, and He makes this provision, and the only right thing is to follow this and withdraw from iniquity and separate from vessels to dishonour. You might almost say that this verse I read comes in after the crisis, after recovery in a sense has been achieved as far as the passage goes. But unless these divine highways are maintained with us, unless we are among those that love righteousness—love what is right—there is bound to be a weakening. The enemy will bring in a weakening. We might maintain that we stand on the ground of what is right, positionally right, and yet we might not apply it in our own circumstances, and allow the deviating and destructive effects of the enemy’s activities that would introduce something, no matter how small it might be, that was not right. Well, we have to be right. This passage would apply to our assembly relations. Our matters in the fellowship are to be right. Assembly matters, assembly judgments, assembly relationships, are to be right; in spite of all the weakness and all that the enemy has brought in, the word is plain to us that we are to pursue righteousness, to do what is right, no matter what others may do.

Then, of course, if we are following righteousness we shall certainly need faith. These four things would go together. It is not that one is exactly first although righteousness, of course, is the leader. Righteousness is the main matter—and then we need faith—“Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee”. The following of righteousness, doing what is right, involves sorrow and difficulty, involves facing problems, and suffering,

but “Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee”. There is faith in God that, in spite of all the weakness and all the outward circumstances. He will stand by what is right. He always has done and always will do.
Then love enters into it. We do not put love first. Some might seek to do it, but it is

“righteousness, faith, love ...” Love would know how to express divine things, to express righteousness in such a way that it is attractive, so that it cannot but be accepted. If a thing is right, and if love is in it, then at any rate it is presented rightly. The apostle speaks of love having long patience and being kind and of love never failing. That is to say, love will do what needs to be done and do it rightly. We cannot judge what is right exactly by the way it is done, but the scriptural thought would be that things are held rightly and that things are done in love (1 Corinthians 16: 14).

Peace, of course, is a great feature that is to mark the dispensation. It is what comes in as righteousness is pursued and as faith and love are operating; then peace will certainly be enjoyed. It is not going to be peace at any price. It is not going to be taking the easy way for the sake of peace. There is a way that is right and it is bound to result in peace—“And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and assurance for ever”, Isaiah 32: 17.

May we be encouraged as to these great highways. May they be in our hearts and may there be no deviation in relation to them, but going from strength to strength in relation to these exercises. May the Lord bless His word.

What I had in mind, beloved, to speak about is “the bride, the Lamb’s wife”. The book of the Revelation, as we know, is written in symbolic language; it is a mystery to many, even in professing christendom, maybe to most, but the truth of it and the meaning of it have been opened up to us by the Holy Spirit. It is an interesting book; it covers from time right through to eternity. In the first chapter the One “like the Son of man” who appeared to John said,
“Write therefore what thou hast seen, and the things that are, and the things that are about to be after these” (Revelation 1: 19). What we have here is what is “about to be after these”.
This scripture has in view the great day of display, and what is being demonstrated is “the bride, the Lamb’s wife”. I wanted to speak briefly about these two features.

I think it is quite clear that the glory of “the bride, the Lamb’s wife” is being acquired in this time in which we are. What will shine out then will not be something that has been suddenly acquired, but it is being acquired in the time of the Spirit. It suggests the importance of the day we are in, and raises the question whether we understand the true feelings of the Lamb’s wife. We think of the Bridegroom and of the bride, and we think of the assembly occasion in a particular way, for in it the Bridegroom enjoys the affections of the bride, and the bride enjoys the affections of the Bridegroom. All this would be basic to the faithfulness of the Lamb’s wife during the absence
of her Husband.

In Matthew 25 we read of five wise virgins, and the cry goes out, “Behold, the bridegroom; go forth to meet him” (verse 6). Faithful lovers of Jesus would always have that in mind, it would ever be before them, “Behold the bridegroom”. It is something to take hold of, beloved; we should think of the Lord in this way perhaps more than we do. We can appreciate what He is receiving now, “He shall see of the fruit of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied” (Isaiah 53: 11)—He is satisfied with the bride. He speaks Himself in Matthew 13 of what He was seeking, “beautiful pearls”, “and having found one pearl of great value, he went and sold all whatever he had and bought it” (verse 46). It is wonderful to think of what bridal affections mean to the Bridegroom.

But then I wanted to refer to other scriptures in Revelation in regard to the Lamb’s wife. I think the testing part of the history of the assembly down here is the matter of the Lamb’s wife. It calls for faithfulness in His absence; the Lamb’s wife would feel the absence of the Husband and would be desirous of being faithful to Him in the meantime. That is important, beloved. The harlot says, “I sit a queen, and I am not a widow” (Revelation 18: 7)—she has no feeling for her husband. But the Lamb’s wife is faithful to Him during His absence. As we consider the words to the seven assemblies we may regard some of them as historical, and maybe they are, but I do not think that characteristically they are. I am thinking of the Lamb’s wife involving suffering; and at the present time the Smyrna condition is amongst us. I believe, beloved, it is a suffering time, as perhaps has not been known for many years, maybe hundreds of years; it is not the same kind of suffering that the martyrs suffered, but it is a suffering time. It is a time which calls for faithfulness, when beloved saints are in isolation but going on faithfully with perhaps little in the way of outward fellowship; and then there are the beloved saints of whom we are often reminded in Eastern Europe and in Russia. It is a suffering time and the Smyrna condition is here. But I believe that as we are faithful to the Lord we will characteristically be among those who are marked by the features of the Lamb’s wife.

Then we read the word to Philadelphia and the commendation, “Thou hast ... kept my word, and hast not denied my name”, Revelation 3: 8. That involves the Lord’s authority. His word is what would be current—what has been made known through the dispensation by the Spirit.

We think of divine principles that have been laid out for us, and the Lord’s authority in every local assembly, and both must be maintained. The Lord has His own rights in every local assembly and we should never forget this; no one should interfere with those rights. “Thou hast ... kept my word” would involve faithfulness to Christ. He also says, “Hold fast what thou hast, that no one take thy crown”, and, “I come quickly”. Well, we can thank God for faithful local assemblies.

But there is the other side when we read the word to Laodicea. There it is not the features of the Lamb’s wife; what is said is, “I am rich, and am grown rich, and have need of nothing”, Revelation 3: 17. Independence of Christ, beloved, is a serious matter and it is connected with a local assembly, Laodicea. It is affecting that He has to say to it, “Behold, I stand at the door and am knocking” (verse 20).
I trust that we and all the beloved saints may be affected by what is needed at this time—the

need to be faithful to Christ, the need to hold things rightly in every local assembly, and preparedness for suffering. We do enjoy the privilege side when He comes in at the assembly occasion, and this privilege should constantly stir our hearts to think of Him and His coming for His assembly. Readiness for this would cause a quick response to the cry “Behold the bridegroom”. In the meantime let us be faithful to Him and honour His rights in every local assembly, for His name’s sake.

The Lord is seen here praying, which is a great feature of His manhood. If the first man, Adam, had been so marked he would not have fallen in the temptation (Genesis 3: 6), the result of his fall being that “death reigned from Adam unto Moses”, Romans 5: 14. But all—

and more—was recovered through Him who was obedient—“by the obedience of the one the many will be constituted righteous”, Romans 5: 19. The Lord was marked by dependence in His relations with His Father and it was expressed in His prayers. In great pressure the Lord says prophetically in Psalm 109: 4, “I give myself unto prayer”. What a model for us! Our brother has been speaking of Paul’s service in relation to two localities and his service would include his prayers for the saints. We are given the substance of those prayers in his epistles to the Ephesians,
Philippians, Colossians, and Thessalonians. Paul’s prayers related to these places and that fits in with Luke 11, which we have read, where the Lord “was in a certain place praying”.

This would lead us to think of our own locality and what is fitting in our prayers as learning from the Lord—then extending, it may be, to other places in relation to the testimony. Prayer is to lead to something in the way of deliverance and blessing. The Lord’s praying led to an enquiry on the part of the disciples, and one hopes we may profit from this enquiry and the Lord’s teaching as to the matter. In Psalm 73 Asaph was helped and instructed in his prayer and he came to an end of the matter which caused him concern—“But as for me, it is good for me to draw near to God” (Psalm 78: 28); “then understood I their end” (Psalm 78: 17).

The passage in Luke 11 follows the Lord’s ministry in Bethany; He was in “a certain place”, unnamed so that we might see what may proceed according to God in our localities. The Lord says, “Father, thy name be hallowed”, which suggests that our prayers are to be in accord with divine prerogatives, self-judged persons honouring the Father in their approach to Him—man’s will being practically set aside in such. We come over to the Father’s side, so to speak, as seeing the principles of the kingdom, “thy kingdom come” involving submission on our part. All this clears the ground in our souls as we approach God. The principles of the kingdom will be the same in every place and we do not want anything less than the best for our locality, or any other place where the Lord has put His name. All this is instructive as getting out of our own little circumstances into the divine light for the testimony and then seeing how we are set in relation to the kingdom and the assembly; and the purposes and

counsels of God. People say ‘prayer changes things’, but christianity is that prayer changes us and brings us to a knowledge of His will, “that if we ask him anything according to his will he hears us”, 1 John 5: 14.

A leading point in the instruction in Luke 11 is urgency in our supplications. We are not ashamed to be urgent with God about matters, whether they be household or assembly or personal exercises. The man here goes to his friend—the Lord calls it “his shamelessness” in asking—and he gets from his friend at the darkest hour what he requests. “For everyone that asks receives; and he that seeks finds; and to him that knocks it will be opened”; all this implies urgency—and the king’s business is urgent—and the request here leads to the asking in relation to the Holy Spirit. Room for the Spirit is a great point in our local gatherings and the Father is ready to “give (the) Holy Spirit to them that ask him”.

“Thy kingdom come” would lead on in christianity to the kingdom of God, which is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14: 17). It is instructive to see how the Lord proceeds as a result of the inquiry by the disciples to the matter of the Spirit. We ought to ask the Lord to teach us to pray; it may be we have much to learn. Do we learn anything in the prayer meetings? The Lord is here giving us directions as to prayer, He Himself giving the lead in dependence, showing us the way.
Lord Jesus come—Thy saints are calling Thee,
They call from hearts bereft—and solit’ry;
Just waiting orphans here where Thou hast died,
Who in Thy love are seeking to abide.
Lord Jesus come—Thou blessed Son of God,
Whose grace sustains us here with heavenly food;
In love Thou gav’st Thyself—our hearts to win,
And free us from the power and guilt of sin.
Lord Jesus come—rise up as one from sleep,
Scatter Thy foes who dare molest Thy sheep;
They hear Thy voice—no stranger do they know,
But follow Thee in all Thy path below.
Lord Jesus come—Thy path it upward leads
Out from this world where men in direst needs
Will soon be left to meet dark judgment day,
And righteousness assert its rightful sway.
Lord Jesus come—‘tis ‘whosoever will’,
Thy hands outstretched in grace to save and fill
Repenting ones who come and call to Thee,
And from this evil world and judgment flee.
Lord Jesus come—Thy name be glorified—
Thyself pre-eminent where Thou hast died;
Thy majesty to reign from sea to sea,
And men in blest relationship with Thee.
Lord Jesus come—Amen—Yea quickly come
And raise Thy sleeping saints and take us home
To that blest place in love by Thee prepared
For all Thine own, redeemed, in rapture shared.

A contemporary manuscript says that, shortly before his departure. Mr. Bellett’s great desire was for a nearer apprehension of the love of Christ. ‘Only think’, he said to one near him, ‘I am going to see Jesus! I know that after that I shall be introduced to the kingdom of glories, to our brethren, and have crowns and rule, but this is all bye and bye; it is not that I think of, it is falling asleep to be “with the Lord”, with Himself with the Man of Sychar! with Him who stayed to call Zacchaeus! with the Man of the eighth of John! with the Man who hung on the cross! with the Man who died! Oh to be with Him before the glories, the crowns, or the kingdom appear. It is wonderful, wonderful! With the Man of Sychar alone, the Man of the gate of the city of Nain—I am going to be with Him for ever, to change this sad, sad scene which has cast Him out, for His presence! Oh, the Man of Sychar!
Lines by J. G. Bellett
When shall I rise to Jesus
And find myself but one
Among the countless thousands
That shine round Him alone?
When shall I wear my raiment,
Through Him made white and clean,
No darkening cloud around me,
No hateful spot within?
When shall I hear the music,
Skilled in this art alone,
To sound “the name of Jesus”
Before the Father’s throne?
When shall I see the glory
My Saviour’s presence sheds,
And know no other pleasure
Than what His presence yields?
Note—Touching reference was made to J.G.B. by Mr. J. Taylor in his address in London in 1949 on ‘The Man of the Eighth of John’ (N.S. Vol. 93, p.506)

(The page numbers refer to “Memorials of J. B. Catterall’s Ministry”) One thing that marks the love of Christ, beloved, is its intensely plain speaking, and that touches us in many ways, but in whatever way it may touch our spirits, it always has the great end in view of its own satisfaction, and connected with that, the satisfaction of the Father’s heart. (p.1)

The institution of the Supper, the service of feet-washing, the service and care of the Lord immediately on His resurrection in regard of Mary Magdalene particularly, : and the dealings of the Lord with Peter at the close of His pathway here, are the plain speaking of the love of Christ that will not endure remoteness. I know of nothing that one becomes so accustomed to with all one’s knowledge of the truth, as the tendency to live in heart at a distance from the Lord. To know the things that are His pleasure and interest, to know the things that are changelessly dear to Himself, and yet, as to our personal links with Him, to be remote, could never satisfy His heart. (p.3)
Everything that makes much of Christ washes the saints’ feet. Peace and comfort flow from it. (p.16)
There are many things I may have reached by discipline that I might have reached by feet-washing, but it is the fidelity of the love of Christ that has brought me there in the end. (p.17)
The person whose heart is where Christ is, is not necessarily an unpractical sort of person.

You will find far more help in your difficulties from a man whose heart is in heaven, for the reason that he brings in the light of God’s presence on them and not the accumulated knowledge of man. (p.19)

There are powers you can depend upon beyond everything here. You may say, You do not know my situation; where I am employed there are difficulties arising, and men are making up their minds that if I do not join their organisations, they will carry things to the bitter end.
God has an angel for that. God has an angel for every situation. (p54)

If we were asked by the Lord Himself what we wanted most in the assembly, what should we say? Some might say, I should like to preach; others might like to teach; some, perhaps, would like to be wise; while others might desire to be available to the saints in whatever service opened to them. The greatest thing open to us in the assembly of God’s people is to be like Christ. (p.45)

Our business is to keep near the Lord, to be in our minds and spirits free with Him that He may use us, but not to seek the Lord’s interference to justify our position ecclesiastically. In what we have from God, be it ever so much, if we are not following the Lord in it, what is it worth? (p.49)

You say, I will not leave the testimony! But you will leave the testimony, if you leave the Lord. There is not a heart among us that can be trusted as to what might transpire tomorrow, if tomorrow find us out of communion with the Lord. (p.51)

You give God thanks for the saints; you give Him thanks for the parents who loved Christ before it became yours to love Him, but you have to learn that the light of Christ in your own soul is the tie that binds you personally to Him. There is no room for natural heredity in the things of God. (p.53)

He who thinks to follow Christ must see to it that he is not easily turned aside by a word, by a threat, or by an attraction; such a one must keep his face in one direction only. I remember, as a boy in Scotland, watching a ploughing match, and in ploughing matches they do not usually set the furrow where all the ground is seen; they contrive in setting the men, to plough that they shall finish their furrow perhaps over the hill, so that the end is not seen at the commencement. The man who ploughed the most straight furrow was the man who kept his eye upon one thing, and one thing only. He fixed his own mark and never watched what his neighbours were doing, and you do the same. The greatest power that can be found amongst us in following Christ is to be attached to Him with undivided affection. I do not get in your way, nor you in mine, if we are both following the Lord. (p.57)
Let us not be satisfied with correctness and clearness of ministry without our links with the Lord being maintained in the freshness, and purity, in which the Lord Himself would keep them. (p.190)
